speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE REHNQUIST
text: We'll hear argument next to number 948729. The spectators are admonished not to talk until you get out of the courtroom. The court remains in session. Mr. Herpel, you may proceed.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court, on an October evening in 1988, Petitioner's husband, John Bennis, was arrested for having illicit sex with a prostitute in one of the Bennis family automobiles, and Detroit police seized the automobile. Both Tina Bennis's interest in the vehicle and her husband's interest were declared forfeit under a Michigan nuisance abatement statute. The Michigan Supreme Court rejected Petitioner's claim that the due process and takings clauses protected her and innocent owner from forfeiture.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Mr. Herpel, will you tell us what the record shows was the nature of the ownership in the automobile in question?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: The record shows that the vehicle was co -owned, that is, it was co -titled in—

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: What kind of ownership under state law? Joint with right of survivorship, co -tenants? What was it? Do you know?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: It's a heavily regulated area, and I attempted to ascertain which common law joint property interest is most closely resembled. I found nothing definitive on that, but I believe it's close to a tenant in common.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: How is the automobile titled?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: The automobile is titled in their name, but there's no—

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: In both names or one name?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: In both names.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: In Michigan law, can one co -owner dispose of good title to the automobile?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I believe that that is true, Your Honor, not for the entire automobile. One co -owner—

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: The entire automobile?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: No. I believe that both—

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Could one owner dispose of it?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I do not believe so, Justice O 'Connor.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: But you can't give us any citations or anything like that, or any place in the record where we could ascertain the nature of the ownership?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I'm sorry, I cannot, Your Honor, but—

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Well, it makes it very difficult, doesn't it, to decide this case when we don't know the nature of the ownership, or what rights a single co -owner would have?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I think it—I'm quite certain that the sole co -owner does not have the right to sell the entire vehicle. That much I'm certain of, that both signatures would be required to dispose of the—

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: You can't give us a case or a statute or anything of that sort.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I cannot.

speaker: JUSTICE BREYER
text: Are we supposed to assume—I wondered the same thing. I thought maybe we should take an assumption that the Supreme Court of Michigan—did the Supreme Court make an assumption, namely the assumption that the ownership interest of your client was such that she had an interest that otherwise couldn't be touched. It was her property. She had an undivided interest or some interest that was totally hers.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: That much I'm quite sure of, Your Honor.

speaker: JUSTICE BREYER
text: So what kind of an assumption should we make? What kind of assumption did they make?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I think that they clearly made an assumption that she had a separately protectable interest in this car.

speaker: JUSTICE BREYER
text: So you're saying even if she had—it was just like totally separate property under Michigan law. She has under Michigan law something that's a 50 percent separate interest, whatever that might mean.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I would say—

speaker: JUSTICE BREYER
text: Well, I'm looking for the same thing. What kind of assumption—

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Again, I would analogize it to a tenancy in common.

speaker: JUSTICE BREYER
text: Like a tenancy in common.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: She had the interest that one joint owner in a tenancy in common would have, or one tenant.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: Does one usually hold cars by tenancy in common? What is it in Michigan? But in any event, he is at least half owner. And you can't impound half a car, and you can't sell at an auction half a car. So in effect, your position seems to be that she, because she is half owner, can immunize him against having his property taken. Is that essentially your position?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: No, Justice Ginsburg, we're not contending that the State has no power to forfeit the vehicle. What we are saying is they cannot do so without compensating Tina Bennis, the innocent owner, for her interest.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: But you're not saying it would be enough to give her whatever pittance was left from this sale after administrative expenses?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I would—we would contend, Your Honor, that the so -called administrative expenses, attorney's fees, prosecutorial attorney fees, and court costs and Detroit police costs are not properly assessable against her interest, that as a matter of constitutional law, that it is improper to assess those costs against her.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: Is it all right for the State to say this vehicle is a public nuisance because of its use?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, the court certainly exceeded traditional notions of what constitutes a public nuisance.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: But didn't it—suppose it had been his car entirely. Couldn't they have—would there have been anything unconstitutional about forfeiture?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I don't think the court has to find that in this case, Your Honor.

speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE REHNQUIST
text: We've held in any number of cases that there's not, that something that's used in the course of committing a felony can be forfeited.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I agree, Your Honor, and I only hesitated because the Michigan Supreme Court applied an extremely novel interpretation of nuisance law. But I don't want to be sidetracked on that issue, because the focus here is on the forfeitability of her interest in the car.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: Just before we get too far away from the answer to Justice Ginsburg's question, if the State can forfeit the husband's interest, and in your position it has to remit to the wife her interest, I take it that's your position?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Yes, it is, Justice Kennedy.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: Does the State have to compensate the wife for the loss of use of the property, her portion of the property, while the forfeiture proceedings are being conducted?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Your Honor, I guess that gets into the issue of whether pre -hearing seizure is appropriate, which is not presented in this case. Assuming that pre -hearing seizure, which is what was accomplished here, is appropriate, I don't know that she would have a claim for the loss of use of the vehicle in that interim period, if that is your question.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: But doesn't that indicate the necessity of having a forfeiture provision such as this?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question, Justice Kennedy.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: Well, if the most efficient way, if the only efficient way for the State to enforce its laws, let's say, is to forfeit the offending vehicle, then the forfeiture system is adequate, and all you're asking for is that the wife's financial interest in the automobile represented by her half of the equity be returned to her. Is that your position?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: That's the position that we're taking in this case, Your Honor.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: And in this case it's a 1977 automobile?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: That is correct, Justice

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Kennedy. What kind of automobile?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: It was a Pontiac sedan.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: And your interest would be about what, would you say?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, presumptively it would be 50 percent of the resale value of the car. I believe the car was purchased approximately, the record will show that it was purchased approximately one month before the forfeiture, and she did testify that she provided most of the purchase money for the car, that there may be an opportunity to rebut the presumption of 50 percent.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: And how much was paid for it, does the record tell us that? Six hundred dollars. So we're talking about a claim of 300 dollars for her?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Yes, at least 300 dollars.

speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE REHNQUIST
text: Mr. Herpel, you referred to your client as an innocent owner, and how do you define innocent owner for these purposes?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, Your Honor, we propose a standard for defining innocence that we term the negligent entrustment standard, which focuses on whether the owner knew or should have known of the impending illegal use. The Solicitor General has proposed an alternative standard. We contend that she would prevail under either standard, either the all -reasonable step standard proposed by the Solicitor General, or the negligent entrustment standard, which focuses on whether the owner knew or had reason to know of the illegal use.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: Let's assume the standard is negligence. What could she have done? What if she knew, in this case, that her husband was likely to resort to prostitutes using the car? Would she have had a right to stop him from using it?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I think the standard that we advocate focuses...

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: Well, would she have had a right to stop him from using it?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Not post -entrustment, Your Honor.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: Well, she didn't have to entrust it. It's half his car.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: But if the time of entrustment is deemed to be the time the joint property...

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: Why is there an entrustment? He's half an owner.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I agree that after the creation of the joint property interest, there formally can be no entrustment.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: Okay. Let's assume we're at that point, and she finds out that he's doing these things on the way home. She would have had no right to stop him from using the car, would she?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: That's correct.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: What should she have done in order to satisfy a negligence standard? Should she have called the police and said, look out for this car, my husband may be doing bad things in it? (Laughter.)

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Are we assuming...

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: If we're going to have a negligence standard, how would it be applied here?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, Your Honor, if I may, I'd just like to digress briefly. The focus is on the time of entrustment which, in a joint ownership situation, I think would be deemed the time the joint property interest is created. Now...

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: If she should have known at that time that he was a scoundrel, that would suffice. (Laughter.)

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Yes. I think if she knew of the impending illegal use at that time. Now, post entrustment...

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: Specifically the impending illegal use, it can't be enough that this is not a really reliable person that I wouldn't trust a car with. Lord knows what he'll do with it.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Justice Scalia, I think it should be specific to the illegal use that gives rise to the forfeiture under the statute.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: But in this case, is there any evidence in the record that she knew at the time the car was purchased that he might use it in this fashion?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: No, to the contrary.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: So your position is going to be, if you win this case, that that's the end of the case, that there is no evidence of negligence at that time, and therefore what she may have learned, even if she had known post purchase, would be irrelevant and that that's the end of the case. She's entitled to her 50 % share.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Certainly that's true in this case because the record shows that there is no knowledge at any time up until the time of illegal use. But the Court could pose cases, hypotheticals in which somebody acquired knowledge after entrustment.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: May I ask you a different question? Let's assume that at the time of the purchase she knew, but she was not putting up any of the money and he simply said, I'm buying this car and I want the title issued and so on, the registration issued, to my wife and to me. And he says to her, you have a half interest in the car. Can that half interest be taken from her? On the assumption that she knew at that time what he was likely to do with the car?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I would think it can be taken.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: What should she have done? She had no role in the purchase of the car and she had no role in the transfer of a 50 % interest to her. What should she have done?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, if she had...

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: Easy come, easy go is your answer to that one, I think. (Laughter.)

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: It could well be, Justice Scalia. I think that...

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: You answered a question. You said this vehicle was purchased for $600. So what we're talking about, you have conceded she doesn't get the car. The state can take the car. So as a matter of constitutional right, your argument is she's entitled to half the value. Well, if she bought it, the total price was $600 and they had it even for a day, then the value was less than $600, isn't it?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I guess it depends on how good a bargain they struck initially, Your Honor. But certainly that $600 is evidence of its value. I don't know that it's conclusive evidence that perhaps...

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: When you said at least $600 or at least $300, that means you're assuming they made a very good bargain.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I guess what I was referring to there, Your Honor, is I think in a tenancy in common situation, which I analogize this to, there's a presumption...

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: Why do you say joint tenancy? Why do you pick the phrase tenancy in common?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Because I don't believe there are rights of survivorship that attach under the Michigan automobile registration statute. So

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: suppose that a state had a statute which said that any registered owner of an automobile is absolutely liable for damage that the automobile does in a collision. And the husband gets in a collision. Is the wife subject to liability consistently with the Constitution?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I think the Court has taken for granted the constitutionality of those so -called civil liability statutes for automobile owners.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: Why should this case be different?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: It's different in two critical respects, Justice Kennedy. First, such statutes arise in the tort system and are designed not to punish, but simply to shift losses so as to facilitate tort recoveries by plaintiffs to compensate for injury. Second, and then perhaps most important, generally speaking, the state would not be the plaintiff in such an action. And the full machinery of the state with its potential for oppression is not arrayed against the individual.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: Well, the state's the one that passed the statute. There's clearly state action in my hypothetical. Isn't the liability that the wife is subject to in my hypothetical much greater, potentially, than the liability here? The liability here is limited to the amount of her interest in the automobile. Well,

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: the liability is greater, Your Honor, and there is state action of the kind recognized in Shelley v. Kramer and in New York Times v. Sullivan. But I think that that is really a this type of state action is quite a bit different. I mean, a civil law providing a forum in the way of a civil lawsuit providing a forum for private parties to remediate.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: We're asking about the validity of the statute. I wouldn't be deterred by the state action. You just have to assume that there is a constitutional defense against strict liability if there is an overreaching on the part of the state by enacting the statute. You seem to assume that the statute that I gave you was quite proper, and I want to know what the difference is between the two cases.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, again, I'd emphasize, Your Honor, that that statute does not impose punishment and, more importantly...

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: Ah, so it's punishment.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: And the state is not benefiting in a pecuniary sense. The full power and machinery of the state is not being arrayed against an individual. Now, in the vicarious liability... That's

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: not being arrayed against the individual, at least in the early forms of the common law. It's being arrayed against the thing, the car.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: That is correct, Your Honor, and I think the Court took an opportunity in Austin two terms ago to begin to decrease reliance on the so -called guilty property fiction that is associated with that. And I think the Court should continue to de -emphasize reliance on that antiquated notion.

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: In the admiralty area, as well as in the automobile area?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: No, Justice Kennedy, not necessarily. I think classic in -rem forfeiture, as indicated in the brief, arose in the admiralty and customs area, and it arose because of a difficulty in obtaining in -personum jurisdiction over, say, owners of vessels. In order for the government to satisfy claims against vessel owners.

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: It could hold it until the claim was satisfied, couldn't it, and then redeliver the ship to the person who ... right? But it didn't do that. You couldn't redeem the ship. It seized the ship. It was gone.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: If the owner was a United States national, I don't know that that would be a practicable solution.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: Wasn't there a very ancient idea that the thing was indeed the wrong doer? I think you acknowledge that in your brief. The thing here is declared, the car is declared a public nuisance.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear your question.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: Isn't there, you were saying the thing was only security for the claim because you couldn't get personal jurisdiction over the individual. But there was an ancient notion that the thing itself is the wrong doer. As Michigan calls it here, the thing, the car, is a public nuisance.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, that's the guilty property

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: section.

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: The

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: deal there. Yes. The idea that an inanimate object you can ascribe guilt to an inanimate object.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: And you say that notion is no longer balanced at all?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, I think it's a it is a it's a rather obsolete notion. It's one that is it's a convenient rationale for use of a civil forfeiture power. And I suggested that the

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: process but is no longer. Is that it?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Your honor, I think that.

speaker: JUSTICE STEVENS
text: Well, didn't we say in Austin that never took hold in the United States? It was an English fiction.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: The Diodan? Yeah. Yeah, we did say that about the Diodan. In fact, I guess we what the court said in Austin was that the Diodan, which actually was rejected by the English Parliament, I believe, by an act in 1846, did not take hold here. And what instead, this the practice here has really derived from the English navigation statutes. And once again, that the law review literature, the historical literature suggests that those English navigation acts were based on the difficulty in obtaining in -personum jurisdiction over owners. And cargo and in some cases ships were seized to satisfy claims arising out of customs violence.

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: That would be a good argument in every case except one involving a car. Don't you have the same problem on the car?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I don't think so.

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: Well, let's assume you have a negligent owner who negligently entrusted it, as you're willing to acknowledge would render him properly punishable. Why can't the state say, I'm not going to go running down where the owner is. I'm going to grab the car. He can come back and make his argument that he wasn't negligent. But meanwhile, you know, I think he's negligent. I'm taking his car. Like a ship.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: The state has the automobiles, registration and titling of automobiles is heavily regulated. We actually use paper title in, I believe, in every state for car ownership. Out of state

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: car. And why should Michigan have to go run into some other car? He's going to say, if there's a crime committed in a car, we think cars are like ships in that regard. We're just going to grab the car. We'll sort it all out later.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Your Honor, I don't accept the analogy because it seems to me that there are other remedies available to the state. In fact, in this case, the state pursued a separate criminal action.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: How does this relate to the many cases where the vehicle that's carrying the contraband is taken. Now, the federal government is heavily into that business, too. Does your argument mean that every time a car is found loaded with drugs, that if there is a co -owner, then the co -owner has to be compensated for the confiscation of the vehicle that carries the contraband, boat, car?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: If the assumption of your hypothetical is that the co -owner neither knew nor should have known of the illegal use...

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: We're not dealing with this unusual Michigan statute making cars public nuisances. Your argument would cover the waterfront of all the confiscation of vehicles carrying contraband. Is that not right?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, or used for some illegal purpose. I want to emphasize, however, that my standard does not address the forfeitability of proceeds realized from illegal activity.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: How is your theory consistent with what this court upheld in Calero Toledo? The leasing of a yacht and the people who leased it had marijuana on board, and the lessor didn't know that. In fact, it even included provisions in the lease agreement that wouldn't be done. And yet, the forfeiture was upheld. Now, how would your theory play out there?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Justice O 'Connor, the court in Calero Toledo did reach the facial challenge. It rejected the facial challenge of the Puerto Rican statute, but the court never decided whether the yacht owner did or did not satisfy the negligence prong of the dicta. You're asking me, I don't know if there was enough of a factual development in that case to really answer your question.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Well, certainly the court upheld the seizure and the forfeiture against a takings claim by the owner.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: They did, but there is a bit of an ambiguity in the court's resolution of the as -applied challenge, assuming that there wasn't an as -applied challenge.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Well, in any event, under your theory, it would not be possible to uphold a forfeiture in the Calero Toledo situation.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, if the facts were that at the time of entrustment, the yacht leasing company, neither knew nor should have known, that

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: the people leasing it were going to have marijuana on board.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Yes, and I think it was Justice Douglas's dissent in that case pointed out that it was two marijuana cigarettes. That's correct.

speaker: JUSTICE BREYER
text: There was also a statement (Laughter.) which I had here that they made a point of the fact that no allegation has been made or proof offered that the owner did all that it reasonably could to avoid having its property put to an unlawful use. And then there was a suggestion in dicta that had that been done, that they might have reached a contrary result. Am I reading it correctly?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Yes, Your Honor. I think that there's a sense in which there was a procedural default in that case.

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: Why is there a suggestion that a contrary result would be reached? Because earlier in that case, hadn't it been said, we've never found that there was any kind of fault requirement, that there was any kind of innocent owner innocent objection. Wasn't there at first that general statement?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, the court did a rather lengthy historical analysis of Diodan's. But I think, Your Honor, what's critical here is that the court in Austin did its own historical analysis and concluded that forfeiture has traditionally served at least in part as punishment for personal culpability. And I think that that history ...

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: Does it follow from your argument that there cannot be any criminal punishment without at least negligence? You could have no no, absolute liability, absolute criminal liability? If your corporation does such a thing, you will be fined so much money, period. Up to you to make sure it doesn't, we don't care how careful you've been, absolute liability. Doesn't that follow from your argument? In the

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: limited to the forfeiture context or outside?

speaker: JUSTICE SCALIA
text: What's the difference whether it's a forfeiture or a fine? I mean, it seems to me the essence of your argument is you shouldn't punish somebody who hasn't been, who hasn't been blameworthy. If you can punish him by cannot punish him by a forfeiture, why can you punish him by a fine?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, it's it's really a species of vicarious punitive liability that we're talking about here, not just strict liability, Justice Scalia. And vicarious liability, punitive liability, or vicarious criminal liability, is a very narrow, occupies a very narrow niche in our legal tradition. Now, in the corporate area,

speaker: JUSTICE KENNEDY
text: highly regulated industries and automobiles, one of the most highly regulated forms of instrumentalities in our whole system.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, in the corporate area, I think in a case called New York Central, the court did recognize that a corporation, which after all can only speak through its agents, it can only speak and think through its agents, can be liable, and some have regarded that as a form of a vicarious criminal liability. But vicarious criminal liability outside the corporate context is exceedingly rare in our jurisprudence.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Well, do we look at this as criminal liability here? Is that how we should analyze it?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I think we have to view it as punitive, that the sanction is punitive. The Austin decision makes that absolutely clear. The sanction of forfeiture is punitive. And earlier decisions of this court in one 1958 Plymouth sedan, which held that the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule applies to civil forfeiture proceedings, and United States coin and currency, which held that the Fifth Amendment privilege against self -incrimination applies to forfeiture, have treated forfeiture as criminal or quasi -criminal.

speaker: JUSTICE O'CONNOR
text: Is it at least possible that in the context of joint ownership of an automobile by a husband and wife that we should presume knowledge by each as to the use by the other, and then put any burden on the innocent spouse to prove otherwise?

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Your Honor, if this is a presumptive taking under the takings clause, as we contend it is, then as a matter of straightforward constitutional analysis, the burden of proving any exception to the requirement to pay compensation would have to lie with the State.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: I understand that you don't agree that mere knowledge would be enough anyway. You don't agree that mere knowledge by one spouse that the other was going to use or was using the vehicle in a way here that would constitute a nuisance would be sufficient for. Well,

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: I think at the time of entrustment...

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: You're saying it has to be knowledge at the time they bought the car.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Or if it's a case of solely owned property simply being loaned, that would be the case.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: Oh, but that's a case in which there's a right of control. The problem comes because there's no right of control here.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Well, that's right, Your Honor.

speaker: JUSTICE SOUTER
text: But to whom there is none, under Michigan law.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Certainly, and that's why at the time of entrustment, at the time of the creation of the joint property interest, one could say there may be an element of control over whether you entered the joint property. That's why

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: it wouldn't satisfy your position if the State law were when there's this joint ownership situation, the court is going to make the wrongdoing owner pay the other one. It's not going to come out of the State's pocket, not out of the people's pocket. But if she wants to bring a claim against him, he's going to have to pay. How about that? That would take care of her need, compensating her.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: You're postulating that she would have a remedy in a court of law against

speaker: JUSTICE GINSBURG
text: John? The State says she ought to be compensated. The car was a nuisance. He ought to compensate her.

speaker: MR. HERPEL
text: Your Honor, it seems to me that it's hardly reasonable after Tina Bennis, an innocent owner, has been punished by having her property interest confiscated. But that may not necessarily be true if a different offense is involved, such as ongoing drug trafficking. But

What else should we look at to determine whether she has taken every reasonable step to preserve her innocence for constitutional purposes?

One, (Laughter.) what is reasonable depends on the circumstances of every case and it is easier to understand my answer, I think, in the fact situation that comes up all too frequently, I am sorry to say, in federal cases where the husband is dealing drugs using the car or the house to deal the drugs and the wife has knowledge of that. And in those cases, the federal government does indeed take the position that the wife is obligated in order to protect her property interests in order to be able to assert an innocent owner defense to notify the police.
